title: The Three Princes of China and the Jade Mirror
summary: The Emperor of China, reaching his eightieth year, gathered his three sons to determine the succession. He handed them a sacred ancestral heirloom, the Jade Mirror of Truth, say...
full_text:
The Emperor of China, reaching his eightieth year, gathered his three sons to determine the succession.
He handed them a sacred ancestral heirloom, the Jade Mirror of Truth, saying:
'Travel through the four corners of our empire for one year. Whosoever performs the deed that reflects the purest radiance in this mirror shall be crowned Emperor.'

The eldest prince, Prince Kang, led a great legion to the northern frontiers, defeated a fierce horde of barbarians, built a fortress of stone, and returned proud of his military glory.
When he held the Jade Mirror, the surface remained dull and clouded with the smoke of burning villages.

The second prince, Prince Bao, journeyed to the southern ports, established vast maritime trading routes, brought back shiploads of pearls and silk, and filled the imperial vaults with gold.
When he looked into the mirror, it reflected only cold metal and the shadows of weary miners.

The youngest prince, Prince Ming, traveled alone on foot through the central provinces, which had been devastated by a catastrophic flood of the Yellow River.
Finding thousands of displaced peasant families starving, Ming did not build fortresses or hoard gold. He rolled up his silk sleeves, helped the villagers drain flooded fields, rebuilt dikes with his own hands, distributed imperial grain stores, and taught farmers to plant fast-growing rice.
For a whole year he lived on boiled millet, sleeping in thatch huts among the villagers.

When Prince Ming returned to the palace in his stained linen tunic, he held the Jade Mirror before his father.
Instantly, the jade burst into a blinding, celestial luminescence that filled the imperial diwan with golden light! In the mirror shone the smiling faces of ten thousand children who had been saved from starvation.

The Emperor stood up with tears of reverence:
'My son, conquests destroy and gold tarnishes, but relieving the suffering of the innocent is the eternal light of Heaven. Thou art our true Emperor.'

Ming was crowned Emperor of China, ruling with deep compassion and ushering in an era of peace and abundance remembered as the Golden Age.
moral: The true measure of a ruler is not military conquest or wealth, but the capacity to alleviate human suffering.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Three Princes of China"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.
